summary: Recommends a minimal set of transport services that end systems should offer and gives guidance on choosing among available mechanisms and protocols. It builds on the transport features in RFC 8303. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8923 asks what a modern network stack should let an application ask for, rather than making the application pick TCP or UDP and inherit that choice. It works through the transport features of the existing protocols, throws out the ones a stack can handle on its own, and keeps a small list that can be built on top of TCP or UDP. It also gives a decision tree for choosing which protocol to use.

questions: what transport services should end systems provide
what is the minimal set of transport services
how can an application request specific transport features
what protocols can implement the minimal set
subtitle: The smallest set of transport capabilities an application should be able to ask for, so it is not tied to one protocol.

tldr.problem: Applications today ask for TCP or UDP and are then bound to whatever that protocol can do, so a network stack cannot use a better transport even when the application would not need its extra guarantees.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC builds a list of transport features from the surveys of TCP, MPTCP, UDP, UDP-Lite, SCTP and LEDBAT, sorts them into functional, optimizing and automatable, and reduces the list to what can be implemented over TCP or UDP.
tldr.outcome: The result is a minimal set that end systems should offer, covering establishment, maintenance, termination and data transfer, with a decision tree for choosing among the protocols that can implement it.

facts.label: Protocols the feature list is drawn from
facts.value: TCP, MPTCP, UDP, UDP-Lite, SCTP and LEDBAT

facts.label: Data-transfer feature groups
facts.value: Sending data, receiving data and errors

facts.label: Inputs to the protocol choice
facts.value: Reliability, checksum coverage, message priority and early timeout notifications

today: RFC 8923 is an Informational document from October 2020 that no RFC obsoletes or updates. It remains the reference for what a transport system should expose to applications, and the interface it describes is the subject of the Transport Services Working Group.

sections.title: Why a Minimal Set of Transport Services
sections.content:
The set of transport services that most applications use is based on TCP and UDP, and on protocols layered on top of them, and this limits the ability of the network stack to make use of features of other transport protocols. If a protocol supports out-of-order message delivery but applications always assume that the network provides an ordered byte stream, then the stack cannot immediately deliver a message that arrives out of order, because doing so would break a fundamental assumption of the application. The net result is unnecessary head-of-line blocking delay.

By exposing the transport services of multiple transport protocols, a transport system can let applications use those services without being statically bound to one transport protocol. The first step towards such a system was taken by RFC 8095, which surveys a large number of transports, and by RFC 8303 and RFC 8304, which identify the specific transport features exposed to applications by TCP, Multipath TCP, UDP(-Lite) and SCTP, as well as the LEDBAT congestion control mechanism. LEDBAT was included as the only congestion control mechanism in the list because the low extra delay background transport service it offers is significantly different from the typical service provided by other mechanisms.

Decoupling applications from transport protocols gives a different abstraction level than the Berkeley sockets interface. As with high- against low-level programming languages, a higher abstraction level allows more freedom for automation below the interface, but it takes some control away from the application programmer. Some transport features are rarely offered by APIs today, yet they must be offered or they can never be used; other features are offered by the APIs of the protocols covered here, but not exposing them in an API would allow more freedom to automate protocol usage in a transport system. The minimal set is an attempt to find a middle ground that can be recommended for transport systems to implement.

The set must also be reflected in all network APIs for the underlying functionality to become usable everywhere. It does not help an application that talks to a library with its own communication interface if the Berkeley Sockets API is extended to offer unordered message delivery but the library only exposes an ordered byte stream; both would have to expose it. Similarly, SCTP offers multi-streaming, which cannot be used to prioritize messages between streams unless applications communicate the priorities and the group of connections to which they apply.

This minimal set can be implemented one-sided over TCP, meaning a sender-side transport system can talk to a standard TCP receiver and a receiver-side system can talk to a standard TCP sender. With limitations it can also be implemented one-sided over UDP. The possibility of one-sided implementation may help deployment, but it costs the restriction to services that TCP can also provide, or, with further limitations, UDP. The minimal set therefore applies to many but not all applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Today an application asks for a byte stream or for datagrams, and that choice sticks. The RFC proposes an interface that describes what the application actually needs, such as ordered delivery or per-message reliability, so the stack underneath can pick whichever protocol suits. The cost is that the application gives up some control, and the benefit is that features nobody uses stop blocking the ones that matter.

sections.title: Functional, Optimizing and Automatable
sections.content:
The document assumes that applications have no specific requirements that need knowledge about the network, such as the choice of network interface or the end-to-end path. Even with those assumptions, some requirements are strictly kept by transport protocols today and must also be kept by a transport system.

Functional transport features provide functionality that cannot be used without the application knowing about them, or else they violate assumptions that might cause the application to fail. Ordered message delivery is an example: it cannot be configured without the application knowing about it, because the application's assumption could be that messages always arrive in order. Failure includes any change of application behaviour that is not performance oriented, such as a security change.

Optimizing transport features are ones where an application will not fail if a transport system decides to enable or disable them, but a transport system may be able to communicate more efficiently if the application is in control. Change DSCP and disable the Nagle algorithm are examples. These require application-specific knowledge, such as delay and bandwidth requirements or the length of future data blocks to be transmitted.

Automatable transport features are those of IETF transport protocols that do not require application-specific knowledge and could therefore be used by a transport system on its own, without involving the application.

The minimal set is constructed in four steps. First, categorization: the superset of transport features from RFC 8303 is presented and each feature is categorized as Functional, Optimizing or Automatable. Second, reduction: a shorter list is derived from that categorization, removing all features that do not require application-specific knowledge and those that would produce semantically incorrect behaviour if implemented over TCP or UDP. Third, discussion: the resulting list shows a number of peculiarities that are examined to provide a basis for constructing the minimal set. Fourth, construction: a minimal set is built from the reduced set and the discussion.

Following RFC 8303, the features are divided into two main groups. The CONNECTION-related features are ESTABLISHMENT, AVAILABILITY, MAINTENANCE and TERMINATION. The DATA-Transfer-related features are Sending Data, Receiving Data and Errors.
sections.plainLanguage: Every transport feature is sorted into one of three piles. Some the application must know about, because getting them wrong breaks it. Some the application may set for efficiency. And some the stack can decide on its own, such as which interface to use, and those are kept out of the interface entirely.

sections.title: The Reduced Set of Transport Features
sections.content:
By hiding automatable features from the application, a transport system gains opportunities to automate network-related functionality. System-wide configurations about the use of multiple interfaces, for example, can be better exploited if the choice of interface is not entirely up to the application. Since automatable features are not strictly necessary to expose, they are not included in the reduced set, leaving only the optimizing and functional ones.

A transport system should be able to communicate via TCP or UDP if alternative transport protocols are found not to work. For many features this is possible, often by simply doing nothing when a specific request is made. For some features, direct usage of neither TCP nor UDP is possible, and in those cases even doing nothing would incur semantically incorrect behaviour, so an application making use of such a feature would eliminate the possibility of using TCP or UDP. The reduced set therefore keeps only the functional and optimizing features for which an implementation over either TCP or UDP is possible.

In the list, a feature is preceded by T: if an implementation over TCP is possible, U: if an implementation over UDP is possible, and T,U: if an implementation over either is possible.

The CONNECTION-related features of the reduced set are as follows. Under ESTABLISHMENT: Connect; specify the number of attempts and/or timeout for the first establishment message; disable MPTCP; configure authentication; hand over a message to reliably transfer, possibly multiple times, before connection establishment; and hand over a message to reliably transfer during connection establishment. Under AVAILABILITY: Listen; disable MPTCP; configure authentication. Under MAINTENANCE: change the timeout for aborting a connection, using either a retransmit limit or a time value; suggest a timeout to the peer; disable the Nagle algorithm; notification of excessive retransmissions as an early warning below the abortion threshold; specify the DSCP field; notification of ICMP error message arrival; change authentication parameters; obtain authentication information; set the cookie life value; choose a scheduler to operate between streams of an association; configure priority or weight for a scheduler; disable checksum when sending; disable the checksum requirement when receiving; specify checksum coverage used by the sender; specify minimum checksum coverage required by the receiver; specify the DF field; get the maximum transport-message size that may be sent using a non-fragmented IP packet from the configured interface; get the maximum transport-message size that may be received from the configured interface; obtain the ECN field; and enable and configure a low extra delay background transfer. Under TERMINATION: close after reliably delivering all remaining data, causing an event informing the application on the other side; abort without delivering remaining data, causing such an event; abort without delivering remaining data and without causing such an event; and a timeout event when data could not be delivered for too long.

The DATA-Transfer-related features are, under Sending Data: reliably transfer data with congestion control; reliably transfer a message with congestion control; unreliably transfer a message; configurable message reliability; ordered message delivery, which may be slower than unordered; unordered message delivery, which may be faster than ordered; request not to bundle messages; specify a key id to be used to authenticate a message; and request not to delay the acknowledgement of a message. Under Receiving Data: receive data with no message delimiting; receive a message; and information about partial message arrival. Under Errors: notification of send failures; notification that the stack has no more user data to send; and notification to a receiver that a partial message delivery has been aborted.
sections.plainLanguage: Two filters are applied. Anything the stack can decide by itself is dropped, and anything that cannot be built on TCP or UDP is dropped as well, because a system that could not fall back to TCP would be useless. What remains is marked with T, U or both, saying which of the two can carry it.

sections.title: The Peculiarities That Shape the Design
sections.content:
Because the functional features of UDP are, with the exception of receiving a message, a subset of TCP's, TCP can be used as a replacement for UDP whenever an application does not need message delimiting. Many applications already do this in practice, by trying to communicate with UDP first and falling back to TCP when the connection fails.

For a transport system over TCP there are several features related to sending but only one related to receiving: receive data with no message delimiting. To support these receiver semantics, the document defines an Application-Framed Byte Stream, in which the sending application can optionally inform the transport about message boundaries and required properties per message. Whenever the sending application specifies per-message properties that relax the notion of reliable in-order delivery of bytes, it must assume that the receiving application is able to determine message boundaries, provided messages are always kept intact, and is able to accept the relaxed properties. Signalling that information to the peer is left to an application-layer protocol. An example given is an application transferring fixed-size 100-byte messages with partial reliability: the receiving application has to be prepared to accept data in 100-byte chunks, and with TCP no messages would be missing, which is also correct for the application. The receiving application would separate the byte stream into 100-byte chunks itself, using for example a Type-Length-Value encoding or a byte stuffing method such as Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing.

On stream schedulers without streams, the transport features for choosing a scheduler and setting a priority or weight operate on streams, and the features in the MAINTENANCE category operate on associations, applying to all streams in the association. The interface becomes easier if a connection may be not only a transport protocol's connection or association but also a stream of an existing association, so the system only needs a way to define a possible grouping of connections, after which all MAINTENANCE features operate on connection groups and a scheduler operates on the connections within a group. To be compatible with several protocols, the semantics of opening and closing must be the most restrictive subset of all the underlying options, so TCP's support of half-closed connections, being a feature on top of the more restrictive abort, cannot be supported.

On early data transmission, two features relate to transferring a message early: handing over a message to reliably transfer before connection establishment, related to TCP Fast Open, and handing one over during connection establishment, related to SCTP's ability to transfer data with the COOKIE-Echo chunk. A transport system could differentiate between transmitting data before or during the handshake, or it could assume that data handed over early will be transmitted as early as possible, with before only used for messages explicitly marked as idempotent, that is, acceptable to transfer multiple times. The amount of data that can be sent before or during the handshake depends on the transport protocol, the use of header options, the choice of IPv4 and IPv6, and the path MTU, so the system should let an application query the maximum amount it can transmit.

On a sender running dry, the notification that the stack has no more user data to send relates to SCTP's SENDER DRY notification, which in practice means the entire send buffer, including unsent and unacknowledged data, has emptied, so it is already too late and the protocol has missed an opportunity to send. Some modern TCP implementations include the unspecified TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT socket option, which limits the amount of unsent data kept in the buffer and lets the application be told when the buffer is filling rather than when it is empty. SCTP allows configuring the sender-side buffer but only as a whole, so it makes sense to offer uniform access to both.

On the capacity profile, the features for disabling the Nagle algorithm, enabling a low extra delay background transfer and specifying the DSCP field all relate to a quality-of-service-like need such as low latency or scavenger. They could be offered in a uniform, more abstract way, where the application specifies a general capacity profile, a description of how it wants to use the available capacity, and the transport system decides how to combine LEDBAT-like congestion control and DSCP values. A need for the lowest possible latency at the expense of overhead could then translate into automatically disabling the Nagle algorithm.

On security, both TCP and SCTP offer authentication, but TCP authenticates complete segments while SCTP allows configuring which chunk types must always be authenticated, which if exposed as such creates an undesirable dependency on the transport protocol. For compatibility with TCP, a transport system should only allow configuring complete transport layer packets, including headers, the IP pseudo-header if any, and the payload. The minimal set excludes all security-related transport features, including configure authentication, change authentication parameters, obtain authentication information, set cookie life value and specifying a key id to authenticate a message, and it also excludes security features not in the superset list, such as content privacy to in-path devices.

On packet size, the feature for specifying the DF field yields an error message when sending a message that exceeds the path MTU, which is necessary for a UDP-based application to implement path MTU discovery. The feature for getting the maximum transport-message size that may be sent using a non-fragmented IP packet yields an upper limit for the path MTU minus headers, and so helps implement path MTU discovery more efficiently.
sections.plainLanguage: Several features do not fit neatly. TCP gives the receiver a stream of bytes and no message boundaries, so the RFC defines a way for the sender to describe messages and leaves the receiver to split them out. Schedulers act on streams, so connections are grouped instead. And several settings that mean the same thing in different protocols are folded into one notion of a capacity profile, so the application states what it wants rather than how to achieve it.

sections.title: The Minimal Set
sections.content:
Based on the categorization, reduction and discussion, the document describes a minimal set of transport features that end systems should offer. Any configuration based on it can always be realized over TCP, while the transport system keeps the freedom to choose another transport if one is implemented. In this section, not UDP marks elements that cannot be implemented over UDP; conversely all elements not marked that way can also be implemented over UDP. There may be situations where the arguments do not apply, for example where an implementer has specific reasons to expose multi-streaming to applications, and in such cases the representation in the reduction section should be considered instead.

A connection must first be created, so that initial configuration can be carried out before the transport system actively or passively establishes communication. As part of that configuration an application can disallow the use of MPTCP, and all the maintenance parameters can be set initially, though some only take effect once a connection has been established. Configuring early helps the transport system make the right decisions, since grouping information can influence whether a connection is implemented as a stream of a multi-streaming protocol's existing association. For ungrouped connections, early configuration is necessary because it lets the system know which protocols to try: a system that makes a one-time choice for a protocol must know early about strict requirements, or it can end up in a deadlock, having chosen UDP and later being asked to support reliable transfer.

The document gives a decision tree for this. If it will ever be necessary to offer reliable transfer of data, notify the peer of closing or aborting, or preserve data ordering, then SCTP or TCP can be used; otherwise all protocols can be used. If all protocols can be used and checksum coverage is useful, UDP-Lite is preferred, otherwise UDP. If SCTP or TCP can be used and any of choosing a scheduler between connections in a group, configurable message reliability, unordered message delivery, or requesting not to delay the acknowledgement is useful, then SCTP is preferred, and the question of whether early message timeout notifications are useful decides between TCP and SCTP. The RFC notes that the tree is not optimal for all cases, since an application wanting the sender's checksum coverage, which only UDP-Lite offers, together with a scheduler priority, which only SCTP offers, will always be given UDP-Lite, making it impossible to use SCTP's schedulers with priorities between grouped connections.

The parameters that serve as input to the transport system are therefore: Reliability, a boolean set when reliable transfer, notification of the peer on closing or aborting, or preserved ordering will be useful; Checksum coverage, a boolean for whether specifying checksum coverage is useful; Configure message priority, a boolean covering scheduler choice, configurable message reliability, unordered delivery and not delaying the acknowledgement; and Early message timeout notifications, a boolean covering handing over a message before establishment, suggesting a timeout to the peer, notification of excessive retransmissions and notification of ICMP error arrival.

Once a connection is created it can be queried for the maximum amount of data that can be expected to have been reliably transmitted before or during establishment, with zero being a possible answer. An application can also give the connection a message for reliable transmission before or during establishment, marking it idempotent to send it particularly early, in which case the receiver must be prepared for multiple copies. A transport system can then actively establish communication with a peer or passively listen for incoming requests; active establishment may or may not trigger a notification on the listening side, so the active side is assumed to be the first side sending data. A transport system can actively close a connection, terminating it after reliably delivering all remaining data, in which case the peer is notified. A connection can also be aborted without delivering outstanding data, and a timeout can be configured to abort a connection when data could not be delivered for too long, though timeout-based abortion does not notify the peer application. Because half-closed connections are not supported, unacknowledged data in a send buffer may have to be dropped when a close or abort notification arrives from the peer.

For MAINTENANCE, the system must offer means to group connections, though it cannot guarantee truly grouping them with the transport protocols it uses, so it must ensure that group and non-group configurations are handled correctly, for example by applying the configuration to all grouped connections even when they are not multiplexed, or by informing the application about grouping success or failure. The features that automatically apply to all grouped connections are: configure a timeout, with a value in seconds for aborting connections, a value in seconds to suggest to the peer if possible, and the number of retransmissions after which the application should be notified of excessive retransmissions; configure urgency, with a number identifying the type of scheduler to use between connections in the group, a capacity profile number identifying how the application wants to use its available capacity, with choices such as lowest possible latency at the expense of overhead, scavenger, or values that help determine the DSCP value, and a buffer limit in bytes below which the application may be notified; and a set of values that can be queried, including the maximum message size that may be sent without fragmentation via the configured interface, the maximum transport message size that can be sent, the maximum transport message size that can be received from the configured interface, and the maximum amount of data that can possibly be sent before or during connection establishment. The notifications that can occur are Excessive Retransmissions, ICMP Arrival, ECN Arrival, Timeout, and Drain, meaning the send buffer has drained below the configured buffer limit or become completely empty, which gives uniform access to both TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT and the SENDER DRY notification. For individual connections, the features are configuring a priority or weight for a scheduler, and configuring checksum usage, with a boolean to enable or disable a checksum when sending, the desired coverage in bytes when sending, a boolean to enable or disable requiring a checksum when receiving, and the required minimum coverage in bytes when receiving.

For DATA Transfer, when sending a message no guarantees are given about preserving message boundaries to the peer, and if boundaries are needed the receiving application must know about them beforehand, or the transport system cannot use TCP. The parameters for a message are Reliability, offering a choice of fully reliable with congestion control, unreliable without congestion control, unreliable with congestion control, and partially reliable with congestion control, with the last two optional and liable to result in full reliability; Ordered, a boolean choosing ordered or possibly unordered and potentially faster delivery; Bundle, a preference for allowing or not allowing messages to be bundled, with no guarantees; DelAck, a boolean that, if false, asks the peer not to delay the acknowledgement of the message; Fragment, a preference for allowing or not allowing messages to be fragmented at the IP level, with no guarantees; and Idempotent, a boolean saying whether the message may arrive multiple times, though it will arrive at least once, which makes it usable by the receiver immediately on a connection establishment attempt. An application can be notified of a failure to send a specific message, though such notifications are not guaranteed and send failures can also occur silently.

On receiving, an application obtains an Application-Framed Byte Stream, which in line with TCP's receiver semantics is just a stream of bytes. If the sender specified message boundaries, a receiver-side transport system implementing only this minimum set will still not inform the receiving application about them, a limitation that is only needed for systems implemented to use TCP directly. If the sender allowed messages not to be fully reliably transferred, or to be delivered out of order, then such reordering or unreliability may be reflected per message in the arriving data. Messages always stay intact, so an incomplete message at the end of a data block is guaranteed to continue in the next one.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the proposal itself: the list of things an end system should offer, split into setting a connection up, keeping it running, closing it, and moving data over it. The settings are chosen so that the whole set can be built on TCP, and so that when an application only wants unreliable datagrams the system can fall back to UDP. The decision tree tells the system which protocol to pick from what the application asked for.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Authentication, confidentiality protection and integrity protection are identified as transport features by RFC 8095. Often these features are provided by a protocol or layer on top of the transport protocol, and none of the full-featured standards-track transport protocols that this document is based upon provide all of them on their own. They are therefore not considered in this document, with the exception of the native authentication capabilities of TCP and SCTP, for which the security considerations of RFC 5925 and RFC 4895 apply. The minimum requirements for a secure transport system are discussed in a separate document, RFC 8922.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption and authentication are left out of the minimal set on purpose, because the transport protocols in scope do not all provide them and because they are normally handled by a layer above. The RFC points to the separate document that sets out what a secure transport system needs.

viz.caption: THE THREE CATEGORIES OF TRANSPORT FEATURE

items.title: Functional
items.text: The application must know about it, or it breaks. Ordered message delivery is an example, because the application may assume messages always arrive in order.

items.title: Optimizing
items.text: The application will not fail if the stack decides it, but the stack may be more efficient if the application sets it. Change DSCP and disable the Nagle algorithm are examples.

items.title: Automatable
items.text: Needs no application-specific knowledge, so the transport system can use it on its own. These are dropped from the interface entirely.

viz.caption: THE PECULIARITIES THE DESIGN HAS TO HANDLE

items.title: Application-Framed Byte Stream
items.text: TCP gives the receiver bytes, not messages. The sender may describe messages, and the receiver splits them out itself.

items.title: Connection groups
items.text: Schedulers act on streams and maintenance settings act on associations, so both are expressed as groups of connections.

items.title: Early data
items.text: A message may be handed over before the handshake; marking it idempotent says the receiver may see it more than once.

items.title: Sender running dry
items.text: One notification for both the TCP low-water mark and the SCTP sender-dry condition, so a stack can keep its send buffer small.

items.title: Capacity profile
items.text: Low latency, scavenger and DSCP choices become one abstract statement of how the application wants to use its capacity.

items.title: Packet size
items.text: The maximum message that can be sent without fragmentation is queryable, which helps path MTU discovery.

viz.caption: PROTOCOL CHOICE, SIMPLIFIED FROM THE DECISION TREE IN RFC 8923

root.label: Reliability needed?
root.note: Reliable transfer, notifying the peer of a close or abort, or preserving order

children.label: Yes
children.note: SCTP or TCP can be used

children.label: Message priority features useful?
children.note: Scheduler choice, configurable reliability, unordered delivery, or not delaying the acknowledgement. If yes, SCTP is preferred, then check the early timeout notifications to pick between TCP and SCTP.

children.label: Early message timeout notifications useful?
children.note: Early data, a suggested timeout, excessive retransmissions or ICMP arrival. If yes, TCP is preferred.

children.label: Checksum coverage useful?
children.note: If yes, UDP-Lite is preferred; otherwise UDP is preferred.
